results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Bringer of the Last Gift, Superior Spider-Man and Town Greeter.
results.text:
I built a Sultai (black-green-blue) self-mill deck, and the site accepted it as a legal Standard brew. The core trick is to cast **Superior Spider-Man as a copy of Bringer of the Last Gift** from your graveyard. Spider-Man costs 4 mana, and because you actually cast him, Bringer's "if you cast it" trigger works. Every player sacrifices all their other creatures. Then all creature cards that were already in graveyards come back. Yours will be a graveyard you filled on purpose; theirs is mostly creatures they've lost in combat. **Town Greeter** is one of the cards that fills it: it mills four cards and grabs you a land, plus 2 life if the land is Starting Town or Treno, Dark City.

**The line:**
- **Turn 1:** Molt Tender.
- **Turn 2:** Town Greeter.
- **Turn 4–5:** Lotuslight Dancers. It searches your deck for a black, a green and a blue card and puts them in the graveyard: Bringer, Craterhoof Behemoth and Marang River Regent.
- **Turn 5–6:** Spider-Man copies Bringer. Craterhoof comes back with haste and gives your whole team +X/+X and trample. Marang returns two of the opponent's permanents to their hand.

Massacre Wurm is in the deck because the returns are symmetric: it gives their returned creatures -2/-2 and drains them 2 life for each one that dies.

**Directions I considered:**
1. A plain Golgari Roots self-mill shell with a blue splash for Spider-Man.
2. That same mill shell plus Lotuslight Dancers, which puts the exact Bringer package into the graveyard.
3. A Dimir Midrange shell with its removal and lands, splashing green for Greeter.

I chose option 2. Dancers turns "hope you mill Bringer" into a sure thing on turn 4–5, and the mill and removal cards I took from Golgari Roots (Overlord of the Balemurk, Cache Grab, Molt Tender) still work alongside it.

**Things to know:**
- **Getting Bringer into the graveyard is easy.** You see at least one way to do it (milling, Dancers, or discarding to Bitter Triumph) in about 99% of games by turn 5 on the draw.
- **Drawing Spider-Man is the weak spot.** You have a copy by turn 5 only about 60% of the time. Overlord of the Balemurk can return a milled Spider-Man to your hand, which helps.
- **The site's 0% figure for drawing the whole line by turn 6 is misleading.** It doesn't simulate tutors. Craterhoof, Marang and Massacre Wurm are single copies on purpose, because Dancers puts them in the graveyard and you never need to draw them.
- **I run 3 Bringers, not 4.** A Bringer stuck in your hand costs 8 mana, so the deck leans on Dancers and Bitter Triumph discards instead.
- **The land base runs a bit low.** It has 23 lands, while the checker suggests about 25. Molt Tender's mana and Greeter's land pickup make up for it.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Mightform Harmonizer, Spell Snare and Full Bore.
results.text:
I built **Temur Landfall**, a brew on top of the green Landfall shell from the menu.

**Directions I considered:**
1. A green landfall deck with red and blue splashes.
2. Izzet Aggro with a green splash for Harmonizer.
3. Temur tempo built around Starfield Vocalist, which also doubles landfall triggers.

I chose the first because Harmonizer only does something when lands enter. The Landfall package gives it exactly that: lands that sacrifice to fetch a basic (two landfall triggers per land drop), Traveling Chocobo and Tifa Lockhart.

**Note on the shell:** The checker pointed out that 88% of real decks with Full Bore are Boros Aggro. I didn't use that shell because neither Harmonizer nor Spell Snare fits a red-white deck.

**The plan:**
- **Main line:** Turn 1 Llanowar Elves. Turn 3, keep your land in hand and cast Mightform Harmonizer for its warp cost ({2}{G}). Then cast Full Bore on it: +3/+2, plus trample and haste because it was warp-cast, making it 7/6. Now play Fabled Passage. Harmonizer's landfall doubles it to 14. Sacrifice the Passage and the basic it fetches doubles it again to 28 trample haste.
- **Traveling Chocobo:** makes every land trigger twice, so one fetch land gives four doublings.
- **Tifa Lockhart:** a second creature that grows from landfall. Escape Tunnel can make her unblockable while her power is still 1–2, before you double it.
- **Spell Snare:** It counters spells with mana value 2, which covers most of the removal the top decks use: Abrade, Lightning Strike, Bitter Triumph, Shoot the Sheriff and Get Lost. Keep one blue open on the turn you go for the kill.

**Odds:** You have Harmonizer, Full Bore and a fetch land all in hand by turn 4 only about 21% of the time (no mulligans counted). In most games you win with Tifa or Sazh's Chocobo growing off a fetch land, or a Harmonizer doubling, rather than the full turn-3 line.

**Mana:** 25 lands. The deck has 14 red and 14 blue sources (each counting the 9 fetch lands, which can get a Mountain or Island) and 23 green. That's a bit under the usual Landfall count of about 26 green, which I accepted to support the red and blue splashes.

**Sideboard:**
- Seedship Impact for Agatha's Soul Cauldron and artifact decks.
- Dragonback Assault and Abrade for the Izzet and Boros aggro decks.
- Ghost Vacuum for graveyard decks.
- Spell Pierce, Repulsive Mutation and Surrak for control and midrange.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Airbender Ascension, Bramble Familiar and Appa, Steadfast Guardian.
results.text:
I built a Bant (green-white-blue) combo deck called **Bant Airbend Loop**, and it's a new brew. Its engine is the one real tournament list that ran your three cards together, which paired them with Doc Aurlock. The deck passed the legality check and was accepted.

**The plan:** Doc Aurlock makes spells you cast from exile cost {2} less. Airbending exiles a card so you can recast it for {2}, so with Doc out, airbent cards come back for free. Once Appa is on the battlefield:
1. Airbender Ascension enters and airbends Appa.
2. You recast Appa for free. Appa enters and airbends Ascension.
3. You recast Ascension for free. Appa is on the battlefield, so it makes a 1/1 Ally token.
4. Ascension airbends Appa again, and the loop repeats as many times as you want.

You end up with as many Ally tokens and creature entries as you like, plus a full quest-counter count on Ascension. Aang, Swift Savior (which has flash, so it works at instant speed) and Aang, the Last Airbender can take Ascension's place in the loop, giving you 10 cards that do that job. To win on the same turn, Haru, Hidden Talent earthbends 1 whenever an Ally enters, and Appa, the Aangs and every token are all Allies. Each entry adds a +1/+1 counter to the same land, which becomes a hasty attacker as big as you need. Without Haru, the token army wins on the following turn.

**What each requested card does:**
- **Airbender Ascension:** It's one of the main loop pieces. Without Doc, it still blinks Appa at your end step, so you can recast everything Appa airbended for {2} each and make a token per spell.
- **Appa:** The center of the deck. It makes a token for every spell you cast from exile, and its entry airbends the other pieces.
- **Bramble Familiar:** Along with Llanowar Elves, it gets Appa out on turn 3. Late in the game, its Fetch Quest side mills seven cards and can put Appa, Doc or Ascension straight onto the battlefield.

**Why this direction:** I compared three options:
- Copying the Rogue list's Temur Battlecrier / Outcaster Trailblazer package would have meant a shaky four-color mana base.
- A two-color white-green Allies value deck has no way to win reliably.
- The Bant version turns your three cards into an actual infinite loop with just one extra piece (Doc), so I picked it.

**Honest odds:** If you're going second, you'll have Doc, Appa and a loop piece together by turn 5 about 30% of the time. Having every card in the full win line (including Haru and Elves) drawn by turn 5 happens in only about 1.9% of games, but you don't need all of them. Even without Doc, Appa and Ascension recasting things for {2} each keeps you making tokens.

To find the pieces, Esper Origins digs through the deck, and its flashback costs only {1}{G} with Doc out. Get Lost and Airbender's Reversal handle removal and protect your combo pieces.

The sideboard is aimed at the current field:
- Negate and Tishana's Tidebinder against the control decks.
- Elspeth's Smite and a fourth Get Lost against the aggro decks.
- Rest in Peace and Ghost Vacuum against the graveyard decks (Vivi Cauldron and Reanimator).
- Two more Airbender's Reversal.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Abandon Attachments, Firebending Lesson and Combustion Technique.
results.text:
I built a mono-red Lesson aggro deck, and it's a brew. It plays Izzet Aggro's cheap creatures and uses your three Lessons as instant-speed creature removal that clears blockers.

**The plan:** Start with 1- and 2-drops (Hired Claw, Burnout Bashtronaut, Razorkin Needlehead, Emberheart Challenger). Use Firebending Lesson (R, 2 damage, or 5 kicked) to kill early blockers. Abandon Attachments lets you discard a spare Lesson or land to draw two, which puts more Lessons in your graveyard. That's what makes Combustion Technique work: it deals 2 damage plus 1 for each Lesson in your graveyard, so usually 4–5 damage for 2 mana. It also exiles the creature, so recursive threats don't come back. Nova Hellkite (a hasty 4/5 flier, castable for 3 with warp) and Burst Lightning finish the game.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Mono-Red firebending:** Fire Nation Cadets, Firebending Student, Firebender Ascension and Great Train Heist. This is the only real list that ran your three cards, but it's one untested list.
2. **Izzet Lessons control:** Accumulate Wisdom, It'll Quench Ya! and Tersa Lightshatter. It makes Lessons count for card draw, but it's too slow against the 12% Izzet Aggro and 8% Boros Aggro in the field.
3. **Izzet Aggro's creatures with Lessons as removal (chosen):** I picked this because it keeps your cards at the center while using the best-tested creature base in the format. The Lessons replace Lightning Strike and Witchstalker Frenzy.

**Things to know:**
- **No blue:** Abandon Attachments has hybrid U/R cost, so the deck needs no blue sources. It runs 20 red sources.
- **Banned card:** Screaming Nemesis is banned, so it's left out even though the menu lists it.
- **Fewer lands than usual:** The deck runs 22 lands, while real Izzet Aggro lists average about 24. The deck's average mana value is 1.84, and Abandon Attachments helps you find lands, so 22 should be enough. If you flood or stumble, swap a Burst Lightning for a 23rd land.
- **Odds:**
  - There are 14 Lessons. On the play, you'll see at least one of the 10 cheap Lessons by turn 4 in about 86% of games, and a Combustion Technique in about 53%.
  - The full turn-5 line came up only about 0.1% of the time, with every card in it drawn. That's because the line names seven different cards; the deck doesn't need all of them to win.
- **Sideboard:** It's aimed at the top decks in the field: Dimir Midrange, Izzet Aggro, Vivi Cauldron and Boros. It includes Sunspine Lynx, Magebane Lizard, Fire Magic, Abrade, Obliterating Bolt, Chandra, Spark Hunter and a third Iroh's Demonstration.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Ashling, Rekindled, Sunderflock and Bounce Off.
results.text:
I built an **Izzet Elementals ramp deck (brew)**. Sunderflock's text is the key: it costs X less, where X is the greatest mana value among your Elementals. Its sweep also only bounces non-Elemental creatures. So in a deck that's almost all Elementals, it's a cheap one-sided board bounce that we can cast more than once.

**The plan:** Flamebraider (2 mana only for Elementals) or Ashling (once flipped, it adds 2 mana each turn for spells with mana value 4 or more) on turn 2. Then a big Elemental on turn 3: hard-cast Wistfulness, or Gigastorm Titan for 2 after another spell. Then Sunderflock for about 4 mana on turn 4, which returns the opponent's creatures to hand while our 6/5 and 5/5 flier attack. Bounce Off (U) returns our own Sunderflock to hand to save it from removal, and recasting it bounces their board again. Deceit and Rimekin Recluse can do the same job, or tempo out opposing threats. Twinflame Travelers makes Elemental triggers happen twice, so each one does double: Ashling's flip adds 4 mana, Wistfulness draws 4, Deceit bounces two things.

**Directions I considered:**
1. A four-color Reanimator pile. This is where Sunderflock has appeared, beside Deceit, Superior Spider-Man and Honest Rutstein. It doesn't fit Ashling's red mana.
2. A Simic Ouroboroid deck (Bounce Off's main home) splashing red. That stretches into three colors and gives Sunderflock no Elementals to reduce its cost.
3. **Izzet Elementals ramp on the Izzet Aggro mana base (chosen).** All three requested cards care about Elementals and fit in two colors, so here they work together instead of just sitting in the same list.

**Honest odds:** You'll draw Sunderflock by turn 5 about 57% of the time. Seeing Sunderflock, a ramp creature and a big Elemental together by then happens about 43% of the time. Seeing all five cards in the line by turn 6 is only 4.5%, but you don't need all five to win. When Sunderflock is missing, the deck still plays as a fair Elemental tempo deck with card draw from Wistfulness.

**Notes:**
- No published list runs all three cards together, so this deck is untested.
- The submit tool flagged that most lists with these cards are labeled "Rogue". That label is a catch-all, and its latest list is an Allies deck with none of the requested cards, so I didn't build on it.
- The 15-card sideboard is aimed at Reanimator, the control decks and the aggro decks in the current field.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Insatiable Avarice, Doomsday Excruciator and Archenemy's Charm.
results.text:
The deck is accepted. It's a brew: Mono-Black Demons that wins by decking the opponent with Excruciator and Avarice.

**The plan:** Cheap removal, Duress and Deep-Cavern Bat keep you alive until turn 6, when Doomsday Excruciator makes each player exile all but the bottom six cards of their library. On turn 7, Insatiable Avarice's {B}{B} mode makes the opponent draw 3 and lose 3. Two copies deck them out on the spot. One copy leaves them on 2 cards, and they run out on a later draw while the 6/6 flier attacks. Archenemy's Charm exiles the blocker or planeswalker in the way, or returns a killed Excruciator or Bloodletter to your hand. Bloodletter of Aclazotz is a second way to win: it doubles life loss on your turn, so each Avarice drains 6 and an Excruciator hit deals 12.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Mono-Black Demons (chosen).** Borrows the Mono-Black package: Unholy Annex, Bloodletter, Bat and cheap removal.
2. **Dimir Midrange.** 65% of the real lists running these cards are Dimir. Its counterspells would protect Excruciator.
3. **Draw-punisher.** Scrawling Crawler (each player draws every upkeep, and the opponent loses 1 life per draw) with Avarice.

I chose Mono-Black because Excruciator costs BBBBBB and the Charm costs BBB. The latest Dimir list runs only 6 Swamps, so it can't reliably cast either. Mono-Black gives you 24 black sources, and Excruciator and Bloodletter are both Demons, which turns on Unholy Annex's drain. I dropped the Crawler idea because it also draws you a card each upkeep, and after Excruciator your own library is only six cards too.

**Things to know:**
- **You're on a clock too.** Once Excruciator resolves, you also have six cards left. Excruciator's upkeep draw (and Annex's end-step draw, if you have one) burns through them, so you have roughly two turns to win. That's why Annex runs 3 copies instead of 4. Use Avarice's {B}{B} mode on the opponent, never on yourself.
- **Avarice's tutor mode only works before Excruciator.** Use it to find Excruciator. After Excruciator resolves, you can only search the six cards you have left.
- **Odds:** You have about an 84% chance to see Excruciator or an Avarice to tutor for it by turn 7. Having every card in the line drawn by turn 8 is only about 11% (the checker doesn't count tutors). So this plays as a control deck with a finisher, not a reliable combo, and counterspells from Jeskai Control are its biggest threat.

The 15-card sideboard covers the main decks in the meta: Deathmark and Day of Black Sun for the green decks, Leyline of the Void for Reanimator and Lessons, and Duress and Intimidation Tactics for control.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Iron-Shield Elf, Bloodthorn Flail and Flamewake Phoenix.
results.text:
I built **Rakdos Discard Aggro** (a brew), and submit_deck accepted it. No published list runs all three cards together, but one Rakdos discard list from late January ran Flail and Phoenix side by side, alongside Fear of Missing Out and Inti, Seneschal of the Sun. I took that shell and added more 4-power creatures.

**The plan:** Flamewake Phoenix only comes back from the graveyard if you control a creature with 4+ power at the start of combat. Then you pay {R}. Most of the deck either puts Phoenix into the graveyard or turns on that condition:
- **Iron-Shield Elf** (3/1 for 2) can discard a card at any time, so it's a free way to pitch Phoenix.
- **Bloodthorn Flail** can be equipped by discarding a card instead of paying {3}. On the Elf it makes a 5/2.
- **Ultimate Green Goblin** (5/4 for 3) discards a card every upkeep and makes a Treasure, which can pay the {R}.
- **Sunset Saboteur** (4/1 menace for 2) turns on Phoenix from turn 2.
- **Fear of Missing Out, Inti, Scarlet Spider and Bitter Triumph** are more ways to discard.

Discarding Scarlet Spider or Green Goblin isn't wasted, since Mayhem lets you cast them from the graveyard that turn. Burst Lightning and Bitter Triumph clear blockers. You win by attacking every turn with a Phoenix that keeps coming back while bigger ground creatures push damage.

**How reliable it is:**
- By turn 4 you'll have seen at least one Saboteur, Goblin or Flail 91% of the time.
- You'll have seen a Phoenix 53% of the time, and both together 47%.
- Having every card in my example line by turn 5 is only 2.2%. That number is low because the line names five specific cards. In practice, any of the eight 4-power creatures or four Flails turns Phoenix on.

**The three directions I considered:**
1. This aggro deck, borrowing the discard package from that Rakdos list.
2. A slower Rakdos deck with the Lessons deck's Monument to Endurance as the discard payoff.
3. A Moonshadow graveyard deck.

I chose the first because the other two give up early pressure. Phoenix has to attack every turn, so it works best in a deck that's already attacking from turn 2.

**Mana:** 22 lands: 4 Blood Crypt, 4 Haunted Ridge, 4 Blazemire Verge, 5 Mountain and 5 Swamp. That gives 17 sources of each color, enough for Phoenix's {1}{R}{R}. The deck checker suggests about 23 lands, but with an average mana value of 2 I kept 22. Real lists of this shell average about 22.5.

**Sideboard:** Duress and Case of the Crimson Pulse for the control decks. Soul-Guide Lantern for Reanimator and Lessons. Lightning Strike for the creature decks. Sunspine Lynx and Thought-Stalker Warlock for the midrange decks.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Resonating Lute, Inevitable Defeat and Jeskai Revelation.
results.text:
I built a **4-colour Lute Control deck (Jeskai splashing black)**. It's a brew that borrows the mana base and interaction from the current Jeskai Control lists.

**The plan:** Resonating Lute is the engine. Once it's down, every land taps for two mana of any one colour for instants and sorceries. That does two jobs. It lets you cast the 7-mana Jeskai Revelation off about four lands. It also fixes the black for Inevitable Defeat ({1}{R}{W}{B}) in what is otherwise a Jeskai deck. Early on, Lightning Helix, Get Lost, Abrade, No More Lies and Day of Judgment hold the board. Then you go over the top:
- **Inevitable Defeat** exiles their best nonland permanent, can't be countered, and drains 3 life.
- **Jeskai Revelation** deals 4 damage, makes two Monk tokens, draws two and gains 4 life.
- **Flashback** lets you cast Revelation again from the graveyard, paid with Lute mana.
- **Helix and Defeat** add burn and drain damage to finish.
- **Stock Up and Consult the Star Charts** fill your hand to seven, so Lute's draw ability turns on.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Jeskai Control shell with a black splash (chosen).** Helix, Get Lost, No More Lies, Star Charts, Stock Up and Day of Judgment come from the format's top lists.
2. **Izzet Lessons shell.** Lute has shown up there, but both gold cards would need two extra colours.
3. **Mardu control.** Revelation needs blue, so this ends up four colours anyway, with less support.

I picked the first because Lute's mana fixes the black splash for Defeat, so the fourth colour costs very little.

**Mana:** 26 lands, the same count as real Jeskai Control lists:
- **White:** 18 sources
- **Blue:** 18 sources
- **Red:** 15 sources
- **Black:** 8 lands, plus Lute itself. Four of them are Great Hall of the Biblioplex, which makes any colour for instants and sorceries. You'll have a black source by turn 5 about 91% of the time.

**Honest odds:**
- You see Lute naturally by turn 5 only about 46% of the time, before counting the card draw that digs for it.
- Assembling the whole line (including Flashback) by turn 8 shows up in about 3% of games without counting card draw. That's because the deck usually wins with whichever parts it draws, not a fixed combo.
- Expect long control games, with the win coming around turn 8 or later.

**Copy counts:** 3 Lute, because extra copies don't add more mana. 3 Revelation plus 2 Flashback, because more 7-drops would clog your opening hands. 4 Defeat.

**Sideboard (15 cards):** It's aimed at Prowess, Landfall and the Dimir decks: Rest in Peace, Negate, Pyroclasm, Spell Snare, Seam Rip, Tishana's Tidebinder, Voice of Victory and Disdainful Stroke.

**The plan:** Make 5 mana on turn 1 or 2, mostly by using Ancient Tomb or City of Traitors to pay for Seething Song (3 mana in, 5 red out), and cast Creative Technique. Technique reveals cards until it finds a nonland card and casts it for free. Apex Devastator cast that way cascades four times, so it often hits Call Forth the Tempest. 1. **Mono-red fast mana (chosen).** It uses the Mono-Red Prison package from the menu: Ancient Tomb, City of Traitors, Simian Spirit Guide, Chrome Mox, Fury and The One Ring, plus Seething Song.
2. **Show and Tell into Omniscience,** so Apex is cast for free. That pulls the deck toward Sneak and Show and pushes Technique to the side.
3. **Green ramp with mana creatures** to hard-cast Apex. It's far too slow for Legacy.

I picked direction 1 because it's the only one where Creative Technique can realistically come down on turns 1–2.

**Why it's built this way:**
- **Apex and Call Forth are almost never cast from hand.** Apex costs 10 and casting it is what triggers cascade, so it has to come from a free cast. In hand, it can still be exiled to Chrome Mox for mana.
- **4 Breaching Dragonstorm** back up Technique, giving 8 ways to reveal off the top. Dragonstorm casts anything costing 8 or less for free, including Call Forth or another Technique. If it hits Apex, Apex goes to your hand instead.
- **20 lands, about 3 more than Mono-Red Prison lists run.** This is on purpose: Technique and cascade skip over lands, so extra lands make the mana steadier without diluting the reveals.
- **No Blood Moon or Chalice, even though the donor deck plays them.** Blood Moon turns our own Tomb and City into plain Mountains, and Chalice on 0 shuts off our Moxes and Petals.

- Turn 1–2 Technique runs straight into Force of Will. The submit tool's 0.9% "whole line drawn" figure is misleading, because Apex and Call Forth come off the top, not from your hand.

**Sideboard:** Pyroblast and Red Elemental Blast for the blue tempo decks (about 32% of the field). Leyline of the Void and Faerie Macabre for Reanimate, Oops All Spells and Cephalid Breakfast. Chalice of the Void and Fiery Confluence for the Eldrazi and artifact decks.

results.text:
I built a Grixis Ritual-Phoenix combo deck (blue, black and red). It's a brew: no published list in the last 400 days plays all three of your cards together.

**The plan:** Buried Alive puts three Arclight Phoenix into your graveyard. You then need three instants or sorceries cast in the same turn, and Buried Alive counts as one of them. If you do it before combat, all three Phoenixes come back with flying and haste and hit for 9. The main line is:
1. Dark Ritual (spell 1) turns one black mana into three.
2. Buried Alive (spell 2) puts three Phoenixes in the graveyard.
3. A cheap or free spell is spell 3. Lava Dart costs one red. Its flashback (sacrifice a Mountain, and Badlands and Volcanic Island count) and Gut Shot (2 life instead of mana) are free.

Two attacks plus a few pings covers 20 life. With Lotus Petal this can happen on turn 1. It usually comes together on turns 2–3.

**What each card is for:**
- **Arclight Phoenix:** the win condition.
- **Buried Alive:** puts three Phoenixes in the graveyard with one card. Faithless Looting is the backup way to discard them, and its flashback is another spell.
- **Flow State:** digs for Buried Alive and counts toward the three spells. Once an instant and a sorcery are in your graveyard (Ritual, cantrips, Looting), it puts two of the top three cards into your hand instead of one.
- **Brainstorm and Ponder:** help find the pieces.
- **Force of Will:** protects the combo turn.

**Three directions I considered:**
1. Ritual-Phoenix combo, using the cantrips, Force of Will and fetch/dual mana from the Izzet Tempo menu.
2. Izzet Tempo with Phoenix plus a Buried Alive splash.
3. A Reanimator package (Griselbrand, Reanimate) with Phoenix on the side.

**I chose direction 1** because it's the only one where Buried Alive helps trigger Phoenix itself, not just set it up. The idea is backed up by one Modern list that ran Phoenix with Buried Alive, rituals, Manamorphose and Faithless Looting.

**Honest odds and trade-offs:**
- **Finding the pieces:** you have Buried Alive or Looting in your first 8 cards 65% of the time. You have one of those or a cantrip/Flow State 96% of the time.
- **Win-line check:** the checker found every card in my written line drawn by turn 3 in only 1% of games. That's because it requires all five specific cards, Gut Shot included. In practice any Buried Alive turn with two other cheap spells works.
- **Gut Shot:** the checker flagged it as almost never played in Legacy. I kept it because it's a spell that costs no mana, not because it's removal.
- **Lands:** I went to 16. Izzet Tempo lists run about 19, but Petal and Ritual make up some of the gap.

The 15-card sideboard is aimed at the current top decks:
- 3 Pyroblast for the blue decks
- 3 Thoughtseize and 2 Force of Negation for the combo decks
- 2 Surgical Extraction and 1 Tormod's Crypt for graveyard decks
- 2 Abrade and 2 Kolaghan's Command, which also can return a Phoenix from the graveyard to your hand

results.prompt: Brew me a Vintage deck built around Goblin Welder, Legion Extruder and Sewer-veillance Cam.
results.text:
I submitted it as a brew: **UR Sewer Welder**. It takes the shell from the Legacy "Sewer Combo" deck, the only real deck I found that plays all three of your cards together (2 lists, one a 5-0 league finish), and adds Vintage's power cards.

**The plan:** Goblin Welder plus Sewer-veillance Cam plus Legion Extruder kills the opponent by itself, with no extra mana needed:
1. Get Welder on the battlefield, Cam on the battlefield and Extruder in your graveyard (either can be the one in play).
2. Tap Welder to swap the Cam for the Extruder. Cam leaving the battlefield untaps Welder, and Extruder entering deals 2 damage.
3. Tap Welder again to swap the Extruder back for the Cam. Cam entering untaps Welder.
4. Repeat until the opponent is dead.

To get Extruder into the graveyard: Goblin Engineer's enter ability tutors it there, or discard it to Melded Moxite or Wheel of Fortune. Cam has flash and costs one blue mana. Skateboard gives Welder haste, so the combo can go off the turn you cast it.

**The backup plan:** Painter's Servant does two jobs:
- With Grindstone, it mills the opponent's whole library.
- Naming blue lets Pyroblast and Red Elemental Blast counter any spell or destroy any permanent. Force of Will is in 67% of recent Vintage lists, so this matters.

**The three directions I considered:**
- **Chosen: port the Legacy Sewer Combo deck** and add power (Black Lotus, the five Moxen, Sol Ring, Mana Crypt, Mana Vault, Ancestral Recall, Time Walk, Wheel of Fortune).
- **Blue tempo using the Lurrus decks' Force of Will package.** I passed because a red artifact deck doesn't have enough blue cards to pitch to Force.
- **Welder in a Sphere/Shops prison deck.** I passed because Sphere-style taxes slow down your own cheap combo pieces.

I picked the first because it's the only one where all three of your cards are central to how the deck wins, and the Pyroblasts line up well against a mostly blue field.

**Honest odds:**
- You see a Welder by turn 3 about 49% of the time, and some combo piece or Engineer about 86% of the time.
- The checker reports 2.3% for having drawn every card in the line by turn 3. That number doesn't count tutors or card draw, so it's a worst case. A realistic goal is a kill on turn 2–4.
- Mental Misstep hits most of your one-drops. Graveyard hate, like Soul-Guide Lantern or Tormod's Crypt, breaks the combo, and you'll often face it.

**Notes:**
- **17 lands vs. 20.6 suggested:** the deck checker suggested 20.6 lands. I kept 17 because the 11 mana artifacts make up the difference.
- **3 Extruders, not 4:** Engineer can fetch it.
- **Melded Moxite:** the checker flagged it as almost never played in Vintage. I kept it because its discard puts Extruder or Cam in the graveyard for Welder; Vexing Bauble and Gitaxian Probe can't do that.
- **Sideboard:** aimed at Dredge, Shops and Initiative. I left out Leyline of the Void because it's black, outside this deck's colors.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pauper deck built around Ardent Recruit, Search Party Captain and Springleaf Drum.
results.text:
I built a Boros artifact-aggro deck (60 cards plus a 15-card sideboard). The deck is legal and passed the deck check with no warnings.

**The plan:** Ancient Den, Springleaf Drum and Ornithopter make three artifacts on turn 1. Tap the Drum with the free Ornithopter for one more white mana, and Ardent Recruit comes down as a 3/3 on turn 1. Glint Hawk and Kor Skyfisher then return Ornithopter or the Drum to your hand so you can replay them for 0–1 mana. That keeps adding creatures and artifacts. After you attack with three or more creatures, Search Party Captain costs just {W} and draws a card. Galvanic Blast (4 damage with three artifacts), Lightning Bolt and Rally the Peasants finish the game.

**Direction chosen:** No published list has run these three cards together, so this is untested. I considered three directions:
- **Mono-White** with Battle Screech and the Thraben/Novice Inspectors. Battle Screech's flashback taps your creatures, which competes with the Drum.
- **Orzhov Glintblade**, which uses Cast Down for removal.
- **Boros**, borrowing the Synthesizer deck's package of Glint Hawk, Kor Skyfisher, artifact lands and burn. I chose this one because Galvanic Blast needs three artifacts just like Ardent Recruit does, and Glint Hawk turns the Drum and Ornithopter into extra value instead of dead cards.

**Honest odds:**
- You have a Drum, a Recruit and an artifact land or Ornithopter by turn 2 in only about 14.5% of games, so the turn-1 3/3 is a bonus, not the main plan.
- Most games are a flying swarm that wins around turn 5.
- The checker gives 0.2% for drawing every card in the example winning sequence. That number is low because it requires all eight specific cards. In practice, any mix of cheap creatures plus burn fills the same roles.

**Sideboard:** The 15 cards target the decks most played right now:
- Red Elemental Blast and Pyroblast against the blue Terror and Faeries decks.
- Dust to Dust against Affinity and Wildfire.
- Electrickery and Prismatic Strands against Madness, Elves and other go-wide decks.
- Relic of Progenitus against the graveyard decks.

results.prompt: Brew me a Pauper deck built around Aurora Eidolon, Sandstorm Eidolon and Spirit Mascot.
results.text:
I built a Boros (red-white) brew called **Boros Spirit Engine** for Pauper, and it passed the legality check. No published list has ever played these three cards together, so it's a new idea and not a proven deck.

**The plan.** Both Eidolons cost four mana for a 2/2. Each one sacrifices itself for an effect:
- **Sandstorm Eidolon** (R): a target creature can't block this turn.
- **Aurora Eidolon** (W): prevent the next 3 damage to any target this turn.

Each comes back to your hand whenever you cast a multicolored spell. The deck has 24 cheap multicolored spells to make that happen:
- Spirit Mascot
- Boros Recruit and Battlegate Mimic (their half-red, half-white costs make them count as multicolored)
- Wojek Halberdiers and Skyknight Legionnaire
- Pursue the Past
- Martial Glory

So the Eidolons work like removal for blockers, or a damage shield, that you can use again and again. Spirit Mascot gets a +1/+1 counter whenever cards leave your graveyard. That happens every time an Eidolon comes back, and also when you cast a card from the graveyard with flashback (Pursue the Past, Faithless Looting, Lava Dart). A typical game: Mascot on turn 2. Looting throws an Eidolon into the graveyard, then cheap two-colored creatures bring it back while Mascot grows. Sandstorm then clears the way through blockers, and Lightning Bolt finishes the game.

**The three directions I considered:**
1. A Boros deck built on multicolored spells.
2. Borrowing the graveyard package (Faithless Looting and Lava Dart) from the menu's Madness and Boros Aggro decks.
3. A three-color Jeskai (white-blue-red) or Mardu (red-white-black) version.

I went with 1 combined with 2. Pauper's best multicolored commons are red-white, and the Looting and flashback cards both feed the Eidolons and grow Mascot. I borrowed the mana base and the Bolt and Looting pieces from Boros Aggro.

**Things to know:**
- **The exact winning sequence is rare.** Drawing every card in the listed sequence by turn 6 happens in only about 1.8% of games. In practice it doesn't need to: any of the 24 multicolored spells can replace Battlegate Mimic or Pursue the Past in that sequence.
- **White mana.** The deck has 12 white sources, compared with about 16 in Boros Aggro lists. This deck needs red and white equally, so I split them evenly.
- **Aurora Eidolon is at 3 copies.** Seven four-mana 2/2s is the most a deck this cheap can carry, and the Eidolons keep coming back, so a third copy plays like more.

The sideboard is aimed at the current top decks, including Red Elemental Blast for the blue Terror decks and Electrickery against Elves and the Madness deck.

results.prompt: Brew me a Premodern deck built around Living Death.
results.text:
I built a UB brew I'm calling **"Mass Grave"**. It takes the speed parts of Premodern Reanimator and puts 4 copies of Living Death at the center.

**The plan:** In the first few turns, fill your graveyard with huge creatures. Careful Study draws two and discards two. Putrid Imp lets you discard cards. Twisted Abomination can be swampcycled for {2} to put itself in the graveyard. Buried Alive puts three creatures there at once. Then Dark Ritual, plus Lotus Petal when needed, gets you to Living Death's 5 mana by turn 3 or 4. Living Death makes both players sacrifice every creature they control, then brings back every creature in the graveyards. For you that means Akroma (6/6 flier with haste and protection from black and red), Phantom Nishoba (gains you life equal to its damage), Symbiotic Wurm and Visara (taps to destroy a creature). If you cast a second Living Death, any Symbiotic Wurm you control gets sacrificed and leaves seven 1/1 insects behind. Cabal Therapy and 1 Duress protect the combo, and 2 Exhume are a cheap backup when you don't have Living Death.

**The three directions I considered:**
1. **BG Survival.** This is where Living Death actually shows up in recent lists (3 of its 7 recent appearances), but there it's a slow 5-mana reset at the end of a toolbox deck.
2. **Mono-black Zombie Infestation control,** with Living Death as the finisher.
3. **The Reanimator package (my pick),** using Dark Ritual, Petal, Careful Study, Putrid Imp and Cabal Therapy around Living Death.

I chose the third because it's the only one that casts Living Death early enough to matter. Living Death also sweeps the board, which suits this field: it clears Goblins, Sligh, Elves and Madness creatures, and an opponent's Phyrexian Dreadnought on the battlefield gets sacrificed for good.

**Honest numbers and tradeoffs:**
- You'll have Living Death in hand by turn 4 about 53% of the time. You'll have it together with at least one graveyard enabler about 50% of the time.
- The checker's line-odds figure (0.1%) counts every card in my listed line, but you only need one fatty in the graveyard, not that exact set.
- I run 18 lands, while real Reanimator lists average 14. Their reanimation spells cost 1–2 mana, but Living Death costs 5.
- The checker warned that Akroma and Symbiotic Wurm can't be cast with this mana. That's deliberate: they only ever enter from the graveyard.
- Living Death also returns creatures from your opponent's graveyard.
- Graveyard hate is the real danger: Tormod's Crypt shows up in about 43% of recent lists.

**Sideboard (15):** 3 Duress and 2 Unmask against Stiflenought and the other counterspell decks. 2 Hydroblast for Sligh. 3 Snuff Out and 2 Diabolic Edict for Dreadnought and Terravore. 2 Engineered Plague for Goblins and Elves. 1 Tormod's Crypt against opposing Reanimator and Hermit Druid decks.
